chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Sulayman ibn Khalid said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who had money with him that belonged to me, and he haggled with me over it, then swore an oath [to deny it]. Then money of his came to be with me; should I take it in place of my money which he took and denied, and I swear an oath over it just as he did?
He (peace be upon him) said, "If he cheated you, do not cheat him, and do not enter into what you blamed him for."

key_terms.أَحْلِفُ عَلَيْهِ: I swear an oath over it
key_terms.كَابَرَنِي: He haggled or disputed with me

ai.seo_question: What is the proper ethical response when a debtor denies a debt and swears falsely?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the principle of *la takhun* (do not betray/cheat) by distinguishing between general reciprocity and mimicking the specific vice of the wrongdoer. While the creditor may legally seize equivalent value, they must avoid entering into the same category of sin—specifically false swearing or deceit—that the debtor committed, thereby preserving moral purity over mere transactional justice. This reflects the Shia emphasis on *adab al-mu'amalat* (etiquette of dealings), where the manner of recovery is as significant as the recovery itself.
